title: Vashti refuses (Esther 1)
hook: a queen will not be put on display, and pays for it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the plea near the end of Lamentations: turn us back, renew our days. Your line was renew our days. What old good thing did you pick up again? Today, a new scroll opens, at a party in Persia. Day eight hundred sixty-four.

The party is in its seventh day. King Ahasuerus has already spent a hundred and eighty days, the text says, showing his officials the riches of his kingdom. Now everyone in the palace city of Shushan is invited. Wine is served in vessels of gold, as much as each guest pleases. On the seventh day, when the king's heart is merry with wine, he has one more thing to show. He sends seven chamberlains to bring in his queen. Today's word is what happened next.
screen: `A FEAST IN PERSIA.` → `THE KING'S HEART MERRY WITH WINE.` → `SEVEN CHAMBERLAINS SENT FOR THE QUEEN.`

segments.voice: Vashti refuses. The order, in the JPS 1917 translation, was to bring "Vashti the queen before the king with the crown royal, to show the peoples and the princes her beauty; for she was fair to look on." She's to be brought in and shown, like the gold cups and the rest of the treasury. Then the next verse: "But the queen Vashti refused to come at the king's commandment by the chamberlains; therefore was the king very wroth, and his anger burned in him." In Hebrew it's quick: vatema'en, and she refused. The text never tells us why. It gives her no speech. Just the refusal, in one verb. What follows is almost comic. The king of the whole empire, furious, turns to his wise men and asks what the law says to do with a queen who won't come. One of them warns that word will spread, and wives across the kingdom will hear of it and despise their husbands. So letters go out to every province, to every people in its own language, that every man should bear rule in his own house. Vashti is to come no more before the king, and the search for a new queen begins. Readers have argued about Vashti for a long time. Some rabbinic stories paint her harshly. Some readers, especially in recent times, see a woman who would not be put on display, and paid for it. The text itself just sets down her no, and the cost. And it sets the stage: the empty seat beside the king is where the rest of this story will happen.
screen: `TO SHOW HER BEAUTY, LIKE THE TREASURY.` · `VATEMA'EN: AND SHE REFUSED.` · then, large: `LETTERS TO EVERY PROVINCE.` · then: `READERS STILL ARGUE ABOUT HER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect someone's no. Think of a recent time someone told you no: a friend who couldn't come, a child who wouldn't, a colleague who drew a line. Notice how it felt to hear it, without arguing it again. Then think of someone whose no you might be pushing against right now. What would it look like to let their no stand, without a decree, without making them pay for it? If you pray, you can ask for the grace to hear no well. The bell holds the time.
Vashti refuses. The queen will not be brought in to be shown off, and the king's anger burns. Today's word.
Your line: vashti said no. Today, when someone tells you no, take it the first time, and thank them for being clear. Day eight hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: The book of Esther is read aloud from a handwritten scroll on Purim, in the evening and again in the morning, beginning with the king's feast and Vashti's refusal.

what a scholar hears: the text gives her one Hebrew verb and no speech, so readers have filled her silence in different ways.
